theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: File Streams in Practice

The state bits change only when an input operation actually tries to read. eofbit is set when a read runs into the end of the file. In a file that ends with a newline this happens one attempt after the last item has been taken, not at the moment the last item is read. When an extraction with >> finds nothing but whitespace before the end, its sentry fails, failbit and eofbit are set and the target variable is left unchanged; getline() instead empties its string first. That is why a loop controlled by !in.eof() processes the last word or number twice (or an extra empty line with getline), while a loop controlled by the read itself, while (in >> x), stops at exactly the right moment.

Output: red,green,blue,blue,

pass 1  in >> w reads "red"            prints red,
pass 2  in >> w reads "green"          prints green,
pass 3  in >> w reads "blue" and stops before the final '\n';
        no read has failed yet, so eof() is still false: prints blue,
pass 4  in >> w skips '\n', meets end of file, sets eofbit + failbit,
        w keeps "blue": prints blue, a second time
now eof() is true and the loop ends
Fix:    while (in >> w) cout << w << ',';   prints red,green,blue,

rows: Skips leading whitespace, then one word or number
The whitespace or newline after the token
Characters up to '\n'; the newline is removed and discarded
eofbit, plus failbit if nothing was read; s is emptied
At most n - 1 characters into a char array, then '\0'
As getline; failbit also if the line is longer than n - 1
The unread rest of a long line
Exactly n raw bytes, no formatting
eofbit + failbit; gcount() gives the bytes that did arrive

theoryAdd.text: The standard defines every legal combination of open-mode flags by the C fopen() mode it behaves like, which explains the rules that look arbitrary. ios::ate plays no part in that choice: it only moves to the end once the file is open, so ofstream f(name, ios::ate), which means ios::out | ios::ate, still truncates the file. ios::binary adds a b to the fopen mode. A combination that has no fopen equivalent, such as ios::in | ios::trunc or ios::app | ios::trunc, makes open() fail and sets failbit.

rows: Kept; every write goes to the end
in | app, or in | out | app
Kept; writes go to the end

theoryAdd.plainText: a fixed-size record starting at byte pos is record number n = pos / sizeof(rec) + 1

theoryAdd.text:
Output: 6 7 A 3

f << "0123456789"      10 bytes written, position = 10
f.seekg(-4, ios::end)  position = 10 - 4 = 6
f.get(c)               c = '6', position = 7        prints 6 7
f.seekp(2, ios::beg)   position = 2 (an fstream has ONE shared position)
f << "AB"              bytes 2 and 3 become A and B, position = 4
f.seekg(-2, ios::cur)  position = 4 - 2 = 2
f.get(c)               c = 'A', position = 3        prints A 3
The file now holds 01AB456789

items: Seeking back to the start after a read loop without calling clear() first: while failbit is set, seekg() and every later read are ignored.
Opening with ofstream f(name, ios::ate) to keep old data: the file is still truncated; use ios::app, or ios::in | ios::out (with ios::ate if needed).
Calling getline() right after in >> n: it returns the empty rest of the line; skip the newline first with in.ignore(1000, '\n') or in >> ws.
Numbering record offsets from 1: record n starts at (n - 1) × sizeof(rec), so seekg(n * sizeof(rec)) lands on the record after the one intended.
Reading a file through a second stream while the ofstream that wrote it is still open and unflushed: the data may still be in the writer's buffer.

On an fstream, switching between writing and reading with no seek in between: the same rule as for C FILE applies, so call seekg() or seekp() before changing direction (after writing, flush() is also enough).

theoryAdd.text: To find a file's size in one step, open it with ios::binary | ios::ate and call tellg(). In a text file on Windows each newline occupies two bytes (\r\n), so byte counts of text files are platform dependent; record arithmetic is safe only in binary mode.

questions.questionText: Which standard header must be included to use the classes ifstream, ofstream and fstream?
questions.explanation: <fstream> declares the three file stream classes. <iomanip> declares parameterised manipulators such as setw, <cstdio> declares the C FILE functions and <sstream> declares the string streams.

questions.questionText: In the standard C++ stream class hierarchy, from which class is ofstream derived?
questions.explanation: ofstream is an output-only stream, so it derives from ostream and inherits <<, put() and write(). ifstream derives from istream, and fstream, which does both input and output, derives from iostream.

questions.questionText: An fstream object is opened with only a file name, as in fstream f("data.txt");. Which open mode is used?
questions.explanation: The default mode argument of fstream's constructor and of its open() is ios::in | ios::out, so the file must already exist and its contents are kept. ifstream defaults to ios::in and ofstream to ios::out.

questions.questionText: Which member function moves the put (write) pointer of an output file stream to a new position?
questions.explanation: seekp() (p for put) positions the next write and seekg() (g for get) the next read. tellp() only reports the put position, and putback() returns a character to an input stream.

questions.questionText: Which second argument makes fin.seekg(offset, origin) measure the offset from the current position of the get pointer?
questions.explanation: The seek directions are ios::beg (start of file), ios::cur (current position) and ios::end (end of file). ios::ate is an open-mode flag, not a seek direction.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an open-mode flag of standard C++17?
questions.explanation: Standard C++17 defines six open-mode flags: in, out, app, ate, trunc and binary. ios::nocreate existed only in old pre-standard libraries such as Turbo C++ and was never part of standard C++.

questions.questionText: fin is an ifstream and ch is a char. Which statement extracts exactly one character from the file, even when that character is a space or a newline?
questions.explanation: get(ch) is an unformatted read that takes the next character whatever it is. fin >> ch skips whitespace first, peek() looks at the next character without extracting it, and putback() returns a character to the stream.
Opening a missing file for input fails: no file is attached, so is_open() prints 0, and the constructor sets failbit, so fail() prints 1 and good() prints 0.

ios::in | ios::out behaves like fopen mode "r+", which requires an existing file, so the first open fails and prints 0. Adding ios::trunc gives "w+", which creates the file, so the second open succeeds and prints 1.

questions.questionText: The file log.txt already exists. For which mode does fstream f("log.txt", mode); fail to open the file?
questions.explanation: ios::trunc is allowed only together with ios::out, so ios::in | ios::trunc has no fopen equivalent and open() fails, setting failbit. The other three behave like fopen modes "a", "r+" and "wb" and open normally.

The first block writes AB. ios::app forces every write to the current end of the file, so seekp(0) does not change where CD goes and the file becomes ABCD. Overwriting from the start would need a mode without app, such as ios::in | ios::out.

ofstream always adds ios::out, and ios::out | ios::ate still opens like fopen "w": the file is truncated first and ate merely moves to the end of the now-empty file. So the file holds only X, size 1; keeping HELLO needs ios::app or ios::in | ios::out | ios::ate.
ios::in | ios::out opens the existing file without truncating it. seekp(1) moves to the second byte, so AB overwrites E and the first L, giving HABLO, which is read back after seekg(0).
The loop adds 4 + 5 + 6 = 15. The fourth extraction skips the final newline, reaches end of file and reads nothing, so it sets both eofbit and failbit; badbit stays clear, giving 110.

While reading 20 the stream looks for more digits and hits end of file, so eofbit is set, but 20 itself was read successfully, so failbit is not. good() is 0 because a bit is set, while bool(in) means !fail() and is 1.

After 3 is read the newline is still unread, so eof() is false and the loop runs a fourth time. That extraction finds only end of file, sets eofbit and failbit and leaves x at 3, so count = 4 and sum = 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9.

The third getline reads c and consumes its newline without reaching end of file, so eof() is still false and the loop runs again. The fourth getline empties line, finds end of file and sets eofbit (and failbit), so n is 4 and line is empty.

The first loop ends because getline failed at end of file, leaving failbit set. seekg() does nothing on a stream whose failbit is set and every later read is ignored, so the second count is 0; calling in.clear() before in.seekg(0) would give 3 3.
get() counts every character: a, space, b, newline, c, newline = 6. After clear() and seekg(0) the >> operator skips all whitespace, so the second loop counts only a, b and c = 3.

in >> id stops at the newline after 42 and leaves it in the stream, so getline() immediately meets that newline and stores an empty string. Skipping it first with in.ignore(1000, '\n') or getline(in >> ws, name) would read Ram Thapa.
Offsets start at 0, so seekg(3) reaches D and get() advances the pointer to 4. Moving back 2 from 4 gives offset 2, which is C. seekg(-1, ios::end) is offset 10 - 1 = 9, the last byte J.

Offset 2 × sizeof(Rec) skips records 1 and 2, so record 3 (3 30) is read. Seeking one record back from the end reaches record 4; after reading it the get pointer is at the end of the file, 4 × sizeof(Rec), and the division gives 4.

seekg(sizeof(Item)) reaches record 2, and reading it leaves the shared file position at the start of record 3. seekp(-sizeof(Item), ios::cur) steps back to record 2, so the modified record (qty 10 + 100 = 110) overwrites it in place.
ios::ate positions the get pointer at the end of the file immediately after opening, so tellg() returns the file size: the 9 characters of Kathmandu (<< does not write the terminating '\0').
<< stores the number as the six characters 123456, while write() copies the int's internal representation, sizeof(int) = 4 bytes. With ios::ate, tellg() reports each file's size: 6 and 4.
After seekp(2) the two characters xy overwrite C and D, leaving the put pointer at 2 + 2 = 4. The file is still ABxyEF, 6 bytes long, so seeking to the end gives 6.
Reading abc into the int b fails and sets failbit without consuming the word, so the first output is 12 0 1. clear() makes the stream usable again; then abc is read into w and 34 into b.
The first read() gets A to D. The second asks for 4 bytes but only E and F remain, so gcount() is 2, and because fewer bytes than requested arrived, both eofbit and failbit are set.

getline(buf, 5) stores at most 4 characters plus '\0'. The first call stops after ABCD before the line ends, which sets failbit. After clear(), the second call stores EFGH and then finds the newline, which it removes, so this time the read succeeds.

exceptions(ios::failbit | ios::badbit) makes the stream throw ios::failure whenever one of those bits becomes set. The failed open() sets failbit, so the exception is thrown before "opened" is printed; it is caught and the program continues with end.

questions.questionText: A program writes several lines through ofstream out("r.txt"); and then, while out is still in scope and has been neither flushed nor closed, opens ifstream in("r.txt"); to read them back. Why may the reader find the file empty or incomplete?
options: An open ofstream locks the file, so the ifstream always fails to open it
The text may still be in out's buffer; it reaches the file only when the buffer is flushed or out is closed or destroyed
An ifstream always starts reading at the end of the file
Text written with << can be read back only through the same stream object
questions.explanation: File streams buffer their output. Data are passed to the file when the buffer fills, when flush() or endl is used, or when close() or the destructor runs, so the writer should be closed or flushed before the file is read.

questions.questionText: Which statement about calling close() on a file stream object is correct?
options: It deletes the file from the disk
It truncates the file to zero length
It flushes any buffered output and releases the file, after which the same object can open another file
It must be called explicitly, otherwise everything written to the file is lost
questions.explanation: close() flushes the buffer and detaches the file from the stream; the object itself remains and can be reused with open(). If close() is never called, the destructor closes the file anyway.
open() on a stream that already has a file attached fails and sets failbit, so the first output is 1. After close(), and clear() to reset the state, the same object can open b.txt, so is_open() is 1.

questions.questionText: ifstream fin("data.txt"); opened the file successfully, but a later fin >> x, where x is an int, failed because the next word in the file was abc. Which expression is still true?
questions.explanation: The failed extraction sets failbit, so good(), !fail() and bool(fin) are all false. is_open() only reports whether a file is attached, and the file stays attached until close().

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a correct way to detect that ifstream fin("data.txt"); failed to open its file?
questions.explanation: A failed open sets failbit, which !fin and fin.fail() test, and leaves no file attached, which !fin.is_open() tests. eofbit is set only when a read runs past the end of an open file, so eof() stays false after a failed open.

questions.questionText: Objects of struct Emp { std::string name; int age; }; are saved with f.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&e), sizeof e) and read back with read() in a later run of the program. Why can the names not be relied on?
options: write() can store only char arrays, so the int member age is lost
sizeof e counts only the int member, so the string is skipped
std::string is not plain data: the object normally holds a pointer to characters stored elsewhere, so write() saves internal addresses and bookkeeping rather than a self-contained copy of the text
Binary records written by one run of a program can never be read by another run
questions.explanation: write() copies the raw bytes of the object. For a std::string those bytes are its internal pointer, size and capacity, which mean nothing in another run; fixed char arrays must be used for records written this way.

questions.questionText: In f.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&rec), sizeof rec); why is the address of rec cast to char*?
options: write() takes a pointer to characters (bytes) and a byte count, so the record's address must be passed as a char pointer
The cast converts the numbers stored in rec into readable digits
The cast makes write() add a newline after each record
The cast is needed only when the file is opened in text mode
questions.explanation: ostream::write(const char *s, streamsize n) copies n bytes starting at s. The cast only reinterprets the record's address as a byte pointer; the bytes themselves are copied unchanged.

questions.questionText: A binary file holds fixed-size records of 48 bytes each. After f.seekg(0, ios::end); the call f.tellg() returns 1200. How many records does the file contain, and at which byte offset does the last record begin?
questions.explanation: N = file size / record size = 1200 / 48 = 25. The last record, number 25, starts at (25 - 1) × 48 = 1152, the same place that seekg(-48, ios::end) reaches.

questions.questionText: A binary file stores 32-byte records. Just after a record has been read, f.tellg() returns 256. If f.seekg(-64, ios::cur); is executed next, which record (counting from 1) will the following read() return?
questions.explanation: The new position is 256 - 64 = 192, and a record starting at byte 192 is number 192 / 32 + 1 = 7. The record just read was the 8th (bytes 224 to 255), so the pointer moved back two records.

The text-mode stream turns each of the two newlines into \r\n, so t2.txt holds 4 letters + 4 bytes = 8 bytes. The binary stream copies the 6 characters unchanged. Opening with ios::ate and calling tellg() reports each file's size.

questions.questionText: Which pair of member functions transfers a block of raw bytes, such as a whole structure, to and from a binary file stream?
questions.explanation: write(p, n) and read(p, n) copy n bytes with no formatting. put() and get() move a single character, << and >> convert values to and from text, and the seek functions only move the file pointers.

get() reads every character: "to be" plus a newline is 6 and "or not" plus a newline is 7, so chars = 13. The two newlines give lines = 2, and a word starts at each letter that follows a space, a newline or the start: to, be, or, not = 4.
The loop writes a, c and e (c goes up by 2 each time), so the file holds ace. Each character read is placed in front of s, which reverses the order to eca.

questions.questionText: What does opening a file with ios::binary change?
options: Characters are transferred unchanged, without the newline and end-of-file translation that text mode may perform
Numbers written with << are stored in their internal binary form instead of as digits
Only read() and write() may be used on the stream
The file is opened for both input and output
questions.explanation: ios::binary only switches off text-mode translation, which on Windows maps \n to \r\n and treats Ctrl-Z as end of file. << still writes numbers as characters; storing a value's internal bytes needs write().

questions.questionText: Which situation sets badbit on a stream, rather than only failbit or eofbit?
options: Reading letters into an int variable
An unrecoverable error in the stream buffer or device, such as a failed write to the disk
Reading past the last character of the file
Trying to open a file that does not exist
questions.explanation: badbit signals that the stream itself has lost integrity, for example a buffer or device error during a write. A format mismatch and a failed open set failbit, and running past the end of input sets eofbit, usually together with failbit.
The second open uses ios::app, so Hari is added after Ram and Sita and the file holds 3 records: n = 3. Offset (n - 2) × sizeof(P) = 1 × sizeof(P) is the start of record 2, which is Sita 22.
